newsitem.title: USA: In presidential race, Clinton may win by a blink.
newsitem.headline: In presidential race, Clinton may win by a blink.

text.p: Forget the instant polls, the overnight ratings, even the morning-after interviews. To find out who was really under pressure in the presidential debate, check the eyeblink rate -- and pity Bob Dole.

Dole blinked an average of 105 times a minute during Wednesday night's televised debate with President Bill Clinton, whose average was 48 blinks a minute, according to Joseph Tecce, a psychology professor at Boston College.

Tecce, who has studied the eyeblink rates for presidential debate participants in 1960, 1980, 1984, 1988 and 1992, found that the candidate with the highest blink-per-minute rate invariably lost the election.
People tend to blink more when they are stressed, Tecce said in a telephone interview. A normal rate for people on television is between 30 and 50 blinks a minute.
"Clinton looked very relaxed to me -- he looked like he was having a good time," Tecce said. "... Dole was under more stress last night than Clinton."

Clinton blinked most during a question about Dole's age and how he could relate to young people, Tecce said, while Dole blinked fastest in response to a questoin about salary equity for people in the military.

There were clear signs of the times after Wednesday's debate -- notably the signs hefted by both Republicans and Democrats in what has come to be called "Spin Alley", where campaign partisans give their impressions of the performance.
Minutes after the debate at the University of San Diego ended, spin doctors converged on the media, accompanied by bearers carrying signs with the spin doctor's name.

The practice began Oct. 6 with the first presidential debate in Hartford, Connecticut, when Clinton aides carried small signs. At the vice presidential debate three days later in St. Petersburg, Florida, the Dole campaign brought their own signs, which were a bit bigger than the Clinton camp's.
In San Diego, the signs looked more like the huge standards carried by state delegations at national party conventions.
Only White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry was without a corresponding placard. "I sent my sign carrier home," McCurry said. "It got too embarrassing."

Reform Party candidate Ross Perot, who was barred from participating in the debate, left his mark on the San Diego debate site anyway -- in the form of a huge "PEROT" sign chalked into a nearby hillside.

The letters, apparently written in lime, were written on a hill facing the University of San Diego debate site to give it a look like the famous "HOLLYWOOD" sign in Los Angeles. The source of the Perot sign was not known.
